import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 353

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/353](https://www.erdosproblems.com/353)
- [Er83d] Erdős, Paul, *Some combinatorial, geometric and set theoretic problems in measure
  theory*. Measure Theory, Oberwolfach 1983 (1984), 321-327.
- [Ko23] Kovač, V., *Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume*.
  arXiv:2309.09973 (2023).
- [KoPr24] Kovač, V. and B. Predojević, *Polygons of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite
  planar measure*. arXiv:2412.11725 (2024).
- [Ko25] J. Koizumi, *Isosceles trapezoids of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar
  measure*. arXiv:2501.01914 (2025).
-/

open Affine EuclideanGeometry MeasureTheory

open scoped Real

namespace Erdos353

/--
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a measurable set with infinite measure. Must $A$ contain the
vertices of an isosceles trapezoid of area $1$? What about an isosceles triangle, or a
right-angled triangle, or a cyclic quadrilateral, or a convex polygon with congruent sides?

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

This statement formalizes the leading question, for isosceles trapezoids; the remaining
configurations are given as variants below. The area of a polygon is taken to be the Lebesgue
measure of the convex hull of its vertices.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353 : answer(True) ↔
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A, ∃ d ∈ A,
        IsIsoscelesTrapezoid a b c d ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ {a, b, c, d}) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of an
isosceles triangle of area $1$.

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

Note the area condition forces `a`, `b`, `c` to be affinely independent, so no separate
non-degeneracy hypothesis is needed.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.isosceles_triangle :
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A,
        IsIsosceles a b c ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ {a, b, c}) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of a
right-angled triangle of area $1$.

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

Note the area condition forces `a`, `b`, `c` to be affinely independent, so no separate
non-degeneracy hypothesis is needed.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.right_angled_triangle :
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A,
        IsRightAngled a b c ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ {a, b, c}) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of a
cyclic quadrilateral of area $1$.

Kovač and Predojević [KoPr24] have proved that this is true for cyclic quadrilaterals - that
is, every set with infinite measure contains four distinct points on a circle such that the
quadrilateral determined by these four points has area $1$. The quadrilateral determined by
four distinct concyclic points is their convex hull.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.cyclic_quadrilateral :
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ Q : Set ℝ², Q ⊆ A ∧ Q.ncard = 4 ∧ Cospherical Q ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ Q) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
The answer is negative for convex polygons with congruent sides: Kovač and Predojević
[KoPr24] prove that there exists a set of infinite measure such that every convex polygon
with congruent sides and all vertices in the set has area $<1$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.congruent_sides :
    ∃ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A ∧ volume A = ⊤ ∧
      ∀ (n : ℕ) (v : Fin (n + 3) → ℝ²),
        IsCcwConvexPolygon v → (∀ i, v i ∈ A) →
        (∀ i, dist (v i) (v (i + 1)) = dist (v 0) (v 1)) →
        volume (convexHull ℝ (Set.range v)) < 1 := by
  sorry

end Erdos353

reformulations.difference: The default MeasurableSet condition on ℝ² means Borel measurability, while the papers use Lebesgue measurability.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every Lebesgue-measurable A contains a Borel subset B with the same measure. If A has infinite measure, so does B, and any required configuration in B also lies in A. Conversely, Borel sets are Lebesgue measurable. The actual trapezoid equivalence was proved in scratch.lean as trapezoid_borel_iff_lebesgue. Generic monotone and antitone versions also cover the other four declarations, including the counterexample property, which is inherited by subsets.

reformulations.difference: IsIsoscelesTrapezoid uses strict convex position, parallel bases, and equal diagonals, rather than explicitly stating reflection symmetry or equality of the legs. It also chooses one cyclic orientation.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Normalize the vertices to A=(0,0), B=(L,0), C=(x+M,h), D=(x,h), with L,M>0 and h≠0. Equality of the squared diagonals is equivalent to (2x+M−L)(M+L)=0, hence x=(L−M)/2. Thus the bases have a common perpendicular bisector and the trapezoid is reflection-symmetric, with equal legs. Conversely, that symmetry gives equal diagonals. When L=M the condition gives a rectangle, not a slanted parallelogram. The chosen cyclic orientation is harmless because the vertices are existentially quantified and can be relabelled. The coordinate identity was checked in Lean, but not the full geometric equivalence.

reformulations.difference: The statement does not separately require distinct or affinely independent vertices.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A collinear set's convex hull lies in a proper affine subspace of ℝ² and therefore has Lebesgue measure zero. Consequently the unit-area condition forces affine independence, ruling out both repeated vertices and collinear triples. Adding explicit non-degeneracy changes nothing. This was proved in scratch.lean by unit_triangle_independent and triangle_nondegeneracy_iff.

reformulations.difference: The statement uses Mathlib's angle predicate without an explicit non-degeneracy condition; Mathlib can assign π/2 to an angle involving a zero vector.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Although IsRightAngled a a b holds under Mathlib's convention, every degenerate triangle has convex-hull measure zero. The required measure 1 therefore excludes all such default-value cases and implies affine independence. The Lean proof triangle_nondegeneracy_iff shows that adding explicit affine independence is redundant.

reformulations.difference: The four vertices are represented by a set Q with Q.ncard = 4 and Cospherical Q, instead of four explicitly distinct concyclic points.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Set.ncard_eq_four is exactly the existence of four pairwise-distinct elements enumerating Q; infinite sets have ncard 0 and cannot satisfy this condition. Cospherical means that all points have a common distance from some center, and four distinct points force that radius to be positive. Four distinct points on a circle determine the convex quadrilateral given by their convex hull. The set-versus-labelled-points equivalence and positivity of the radius were proved in scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: Only one cyclic orientation is tested, and polygons are indexed by Fin (n + 3) for n : ℕ rather than by an arbitrary number of vertices at least three.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Reversing a cyclic enumeration by i ↦ −i preserves its range, vertex membership, hull, and side lengths, while exchanging the two orientations. In particular, every reversed edge is an original edge with its endpoints exchanged, so the equal-side condition is preserved. Also n+3 ranges exactly over the integers at least three, and Fin addition includes the closing edge. These equivalences were proved as orientation_free_polygon_iff and polygon_size_reindex; the closing edges were also checked computationally for triangles and quadrilaterals.

review.notes: All five mathematical statements match the primary sources: Koizumi's Theorems 1–2 give the three affirmative configurations, and Kovač–Predojević's Theorems 1–2 give the cyclic quadrilateral and the stronger equilateral-polygon counterexample stated here. The solved categories and answer(True) agree with those sources. The boundary/equivalence experiments are in /workspace/review/scratch.lean and compile with no admitted axioms. The Erdős website remained behind a Cloudflare challenge despite descriptive User-Agent headers; its claims were checked through the primary papers and their original-source quotations instead. The exact external formal-proof source exports matching statements and contains no explicit sorry or custom axioms. However, recompilation against the supplied Lean 4.33.1/Mathlib produced elaboration/typeclass errors, and its original compatible build setup was not available. I therefore did not independently reproduce the formal-proof certification; this alone does not establish a stale-status issue.
